meta.title: Covariance Estimation for Orbit Determination with Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machines
meta.authorsHtml: Benedikt Aigner<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Fabian Dallinger<sup>1</sup>, Thomas Andert<sup>1</sup>, Roger Förstner<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machines (PIELMs) are an efficient alternative to classical orbit determination by combining measurement fitting with explicit enforcement of the equations of motion. Practical applications, however, also require uncertainty information. This paper investigates a covariance estimation procedure for PIELM-based orbit determination that propagates assumed measurement noise through the trained model to obtain time-varying position uncertainties. We compute an output-weight covariance from the Jacobian of the stacked residuals with respect to the learned output weights and map it via linear covariance propagation to a time-resolved 3×3 position covariance along the reconstructed trajectory. Using a controlled groundstation tracking scenario over a single orbital arc, we compare the resulting 1σ envelopes against a classical batch weighted least-squares (WLS) reference. Covariance behaviour is assessed by Monte Carlo ensembles over measurement-noise realizations and over random hidden-layer initializations, using the normalized estimation error squared and empirical ellipsoidal coverage. The results indicate that the proposed method yields structured, time-varying uncertainty estimates whose magnitudes are broadly consistent with the realized errors, while exhibiting a systematic time dependence in the calibration along the arc.

blocks.html: In recent years, physics-informed machine learning has been increasingly explored for orbit determination [1–3], where the objective is to infer a dynamically consistent trajectory from noisy measurements. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) describe the trajectory by a neural network fθ : t ↦→rθ(t) and estimate θ through the minimization of a composite loss [4], where Ldata measures measurement misfit and Lphys penalizes violations of the equations of motion. In operational orbit determination, covariance matrices are an equally important output, as they quantify estimation uncertainty and support subsequent decisionmaking [5].

In this work, we consider orbit determination with a Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (PIELM) [6]. Based on the formulation introduced by Scorsoglio et al. [1], we derive an associated covariance estimate by propagating assumed measurement noise through residual sensitivities with respect to the trained output weights and mapping the resulting parameter covariance to a time-resolved position covariance. Preliminary work was presented in [7, 8].

To evaluate the proposed covariance approach, we define a controlled orbit-determination test case with four ground stations: Kourou (French Guiana), Santa Maria (Azores, Portugal), Weilheim (Germany), and New Norcia (Western Australia). Station positions and local topocentric frames are modeled using SPICE kernels [12]. The observation set comprises range ρ, azimuth Az, and elevation El sampled every 10 s during visibility, defined by an elevation mask of 5◦≤El ≤90◦. Measurement noise is modeled as zero-mean, uncorrelated Gaussian with σρ = 20 m and σAz = σEl = 0.005◦ [10].

As a reference (“truth”) trajectory, we propagate a Keplerian two-body model in the Earth-Centered Inertial (ECI) frame over one orbital period. The initial orbit is chosen to be ISS-like and is initialized from a reference ephemeris at 2023-08-07T12:00:00.000 with initial state vector x0 [13]. The corresponding Kepler elements are

while the gravitational parameter is set to µ⊕= 398600.4418 km3/s2. Range, azimuth, and elevation observables are computed from the propagated reference states for each station and perturbed according to the stated noise levels.

For learning-based estimation, the angular measurements are encoded using a sine–cosine representation to obtain bounded targets and avoid 2π wrap-around discontinuities [1]. Range is normalized by the semimajor axis a0 of the considered orbit. The measurement noise standard deviations are propagated through the same normalization and encoding using a small-angle approximation, yielding

blocks.html: This normalized measurement vector and the corresponding noise levels define the data basis for orbit determination and covariance analysis. In total, the ground stations provide Nd = 191 observation epochs, each containing four measurement components.
For the presented measurement setup, we apply both the proposed PIELM approach and a classical batch weighted least-squares (WLS) estimator to recover the orbit and compute the associated covariance.

For the PIELM, we use Nn = 50 hidden neurons and enforce the dynamics at Np = 50 collocation points. The iterative optimization of the output weights β is terminated once the update satisfies ∥δβ∥≤10−6. The data and physics terms are weighted equally in this exploratory study, λ = 1, following [3], since the normalization described in Section 2 prevents order-ofmagnitude differences between the terms.

As a reference, we perform a classical batch WLS estimation of the initial state x0 by minimizing the weighted residual norm of the normalized measurements ˆy in Equation (18) [5]. The measurement Jacobian HWLS is obtained from the state transition matrix Φ(tk, t0) computed by integrating the variational equations [14]. blocks.html: The batch WLS solver requires an initial guess for the iterative estimation. We therefore initialize WLS with an a priori nominal state ˜x0 = x0 + ∆x. In contrast, the PIELM estimates the trajectory through the output weights β and does not require an explicit initial-state guess. All simulations were performed using our in-house research software, Artificial Intelligence for Precise Orbit Determination (AI4POD) [15, 16]. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 report a single representative realization; the ensemble results in Section 3.3 are obtained by repeating the same setup over N = 200 runs.

blocks.html: Overall, both approaches recover the reference trajectory under the given setup. In the present configuration, WLS yields smaller position errors, while the PIELM-based estimator recovers the trajectory at a reduced accuracy level, most notably in the X and Z components.

To compare the uncertainty estimates provided by WLS and by the proposed PIELM approach, we consider the time-varying position covariance in the ECI frame. For WLS, the initial covariance is propagated along the arc using Equation (19). For PIELM, the covariance is obtained by transforming the output-weight covariance according to Equation (15).

We compare the temporal evolution of the marginal uncertainties via the ±1σ envelopes over one orbital arc. Figure 2 shows that the envelope evolution is similar in all three Cartesian components, indicating that both approaches capture comparable trends in the time variation of the predicted uncertainty. At the same time, the PIELM envelopes are consistently wider than those from WLS. This does not by itself indicate a more conservative covariance, since the PIELM position errors in Table 1 are correspondingly larger. A possible contribution is the larger number of estimated parameters, as the PIELM uses 3Nn = 150 output weights while the batch WLS estimator solves for a six-dimensional initial state. Whether the predicted magnitudes are consistent with the realized errors is assessed in Section 3.3.

To assess whether the predicted covariances are consistent with the realized errors, we evaluate the squared Mahalanobis distance of the 3D position error ∆r(t) with respect to the predicted position covariance Pr(t)

Evaluating Equation (20) along the epochs of a single arc provides only limited information, since the position error evolves smoothly in time and the epochs are therefore strongly correlated. We consequently repeat the assessment over statistical ensembles of N = 200 runs. In condition A the measurement-noise realization varies while the hidden-layer realization is held fixed, which mirrors the corresponding WLS ensemble. In condition B the noise realization is held fixed and the hidden-layer draw varies, isolating the variability introduced by the random ELM initialization.
Covariance consistency is quantified by the normalized estimation error squared (NEES) [17], obtained by averaging Equation (20) over the ensemble at each epoch,
and by the empirical ellipsoidal coverage

i.e., the fraction of ensemble members and epochs for which the realized position error lies inside the predicted p-probability error ellipsoid, with I the indicator function. For a consistent three-dimensional covariance the expected NEES is E[¯ϵ] = 3, with a two-sided 95% acceptance region [2.67, 3.35] at N = 200.

blocks.html: For the WLS reference, the propagated position covariance remains within the acceptance region along the full arc, so the baseline covariance is consistent for the considered scenario. Figure 3 shows ¯ϵ(t) for all three ensembles. The PIELM curve is optimistic over approximately the first twenty minutes (¯ϵ ≈8.9), decreases monotonically, and becomes conservative towards the end of the arc. Condition B follows a similar temporal evolution, which suggests that the behaviour is primarily driven by the ELM basis and the tracking geometry rather than by the specific noise realization.

blocks.html: The arc means of the NEES are reported in Table 2 together with the coverages at the 68% and 95% levels. Since the NEES varies systematically along the arc, these means should not be read as a uniform misscaling of the covariance. A complementary view is provided by Figure 2, which compares the predicted ±1σ envelopes with the standard deviation of the position error observed across the ensemble. For both estimators the two follow each other closely over most of the arc, indicating that the predicted uncertainty magnitudes are broadly representative of the realized errors. For the PIELM, the empirical scatter exceeds the predicted envelope during the early part of the arc and falls inside it thereafter, consistent with the behaviour seen in Figure 3.

Condition B provides a separate check. Here the scatter of the reconstructed trajectories is caused solely by the random hidden-layer draw, and its magnitude is three to six times smaller than the scatter caused by measurement noise in condition A. The trajectory reconstruction is therefore comparatively insensitive to the ELM initialization at the considered noise levels, although this contribution is not represented in Equation (14).
The coverage at the 95% level falls below the nominal value, reflecting the optimistic epochs at the start of the arc. If a calibration step is desired, a scalar rescaling P⋆

blocks.html: This study shows that covariance information can be extracted from PIELM-based orbit determination by propagating measurement-noise assumptions through residual sensitivities with respect to the trained output weights. For the considered scenario, both methods recover the reference trajectory, with WLS achieving smaller position errors. Ensemble consistency tests over 200 runs indicate that the predicted uncertainty magnitudes are broadly representative of the realized errors, with a coverage at the 68% level comparable to the WLS reference. The covariance nevertheless shows a systematic time dependence, being optimistic early in the arc and conservative towards its end. The same pattern appears when only the ELM initialization is varied, which suggests that it originates in the interaction between the ELM basis and the tracking geometry rather than in the noise model. The scatter caused by the random initialization is three to six times smaller than that caused by measurement noise, so the reconstruction is comparatively insensitive to the ELM draw at the considered noise levels.

Future work will address this time dependence and consider higher-fidelity dynamics to assess robustness under model mismatch. Uncertainties in the force model deserve particular attention, since the present covariance is conditioned on the imposed dynamics and treating the collocation points as exact constraints presumes that the assumed equations of motion hold. As the same two-body model generates the reference trajectory and constrains the estimator, this assumption cannot be tested in the present setup. A broader evaluation across hyperparameter settings would further characterize the sensitivity of the covariance estimate.
